items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Heavy rain and flooding across British Columbia’s South Coast prompted shelter-in-place advisories near Squamish and in Pemberton Valley, while evacuation orders covered parts of Pemberton and Lil’wat Nation on Thursday, Nov. 12. Some areas received more than 300 millimetres of rain in 48 hours, and floodwater closed Highway 99 east of Pemberton and roads near Squamish. The entire Village of Pemberton was under an evacuation alert. Evacuation orders also remained in effect in Zeballos, where flooding and landslide risks threatened about 30 properties. The release of water from the Cheakamus Dam flooded roads near Squamish and was intended to make room in the reservoir for more rain. Officials expected river levels to crest Thursday and then recede. Rain eased in some areas, but Vancouver Island remained under rainfall and flood warnings, and forecasters were tracking more storm systems expected over the weekend.

A preliminary report into the post-wildfire hazards associated with the fire has now been released, indicating likely moderate to high impacts on local properties, highways, and infrastructure. A preliminary assessment of the post-wildfire hazards of the Pear Lake wildfire near Clinton this past summer show that homes, highways, and infrastructure such as the CN rail line and a BC Hydro substation are at elevated risk from flooding, debris flows, and landslides in the fire’s aftermath. The Pear Lake wildfire was reported on July 17, and was not declared under control until Sept. 14. It burned a total area of 165,909 hectares (1,659 square kilometres), forced the evacuation of thousands of residents, and destroyed more than 120 structures, including homes. The report — dated Oct. 8 and released on Nov. 9 — is largely based on aerial reconnaissance carried out in August. The report’s author, geomorphologist Sarah Crookshanks, notes that it was prepared on an expedited basis so that a Level 4 Detailed Assessment can be started. The fire affected 28 watersheds, with some seeing up to 99 per cent of their area burned. The Clinton Creek watershed (6,663 hectares) saw 86 per cent of its area burned, with 76 per cent of that burned at moderate or high severity. Some 50 per cent of the Big Bar Creek watershed (45,156 hectares in total) was burned, and 41 per cent of the Maiden Creek watershed (5,955 hectares) was burned. The report states that potential elements at risk include residential structures on private properties; First Nations lands; the Highway 97 and Highway 99 corridors; secondary public roads, including the Clinton-Pavilion Road and the southern part of Jesmond Road; provincial parks at Marble Range, Big Bar Lake, Downing, and Chasm; the CN rail mainline; the BC Hydro transmission line and substation near Kelly Lake; and water resources and infrastructure in the Clinton Community Watershed.

items.title: [nacion.com] Latin American countries raise the alarm over rising diabetes rates and underdiagnosis
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Health figures released for World Diabetes Day show diagnoses and undetected cases in several Latin American countries. Costa Rica reported 17,276 diagnoses in 2025, 28.62% more than in 2024; in Panama, the Social Security Fund treated around 53,000 people during 2025, while an estimated 312,800 adults were living with diabetes in 2024. In Mexico, more than 14 million adults have the disease, and nearly one in three is unaware of their diagnosis. National estimates do not necessarily use the same methods. In Brazil, an estimated five million people remain undiagnosed, in addition to the 16 million who have been diagnosed. In Argentina, nearly four in 10 people with abnormal test results were unaware of their condition. The International Diabetes Federation estimates that more than 589 million adults worldwide are living with diabetes. Type 2 diabetes can progress for years without clear symptoms; when blood glucose remains high, it can cause cardiovascular, kidney, vision, and nerve damage. Authorities and specialists recommend screening tests, clinical follow-up, and sustained lifestyle changes. Costa Rica recorded another 16,758 new cases up to the epidemiological week of October 18–24, 2026.

items.title: [winnipegfreepress.com] Federal memo warns freshwater pressures threaten Canada’s long-term security
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

An internal federal memo warns that growing pressure on freshwater supplies could harm Canada’s long-term security and prosperity. It says it is unclear whether the country can meet future needs as its cities and economy grow. The Canada Water Agency prepared the document for Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin as work proceeds on a national water security strategy. Dabrusin called the strategy a “mission critical priority” in response to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s request for cabinet priorities. The memo links water risks to climate change, pollution, population growth, overuse and aging infrastructure. Public consultation ran from Sept. 9 to Oct. 25, and the agency also consulted provincial, territorial and Indigenous partners. The memo calls for an assessment of water protection and sustainable management, including shared waters with the United States and global water risks. The 12-page memo was obtained through an access-to-information request, with some material withheld.

items.title: [farmer.pl] Farmers turn to soil and water strategies as climate extremes intensify
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Farmers and researchers are testing soil, irrigation and crop-management measures as drought, flooding and extreme heat strain agriculture in Poland, Sweden and Senegal. At a Polish agriculture conference, experts said drought resilience depends on assessing soil conditions and improving long-term water retention. A Swedish research project is assessing a system designed to store water in dry periods and release it during floods. In Senegal, farmers and agricultural workers report hotter planting seasons and fewer hours in the fields, while shared irrigation along the Senegal River has become vital. The Swedish project will test the system under different climate scenarios and develop implementation guidance. Researchers say its effects on soil ecosystems and nutrient releases still need study.

items.title: [straitstimes.com] Leo XIV warns of rural exodus at Mass in the Peruvian Andes
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Pope Leo XIV warned on Saturday during a Mass in Santa Cruz de Succhabamba, in the Peruvian Andes, that poverty, forced migration, and the unequal distribution of resources are emptying rural communities. Around 20,000 people attended, according to the Vatican. Leo XIV, who led the Diocese of Chiclayo, thus fulfilled his promise to return to Peru, made before leaving for Rome in 2023. In his homily, he spoke of those who leave their towns to seek a better future in coastal cities and urged people to confront injustice without violence. Cajamarca, the region where Santa Cruz is located, has poverty rates of up to 40%, according to official figures cited by Reuters. On Saturday, Leo XIV also crowned the image of the Immaculate Conception at Chiclayo Cathedral and closed the jubilee year in Zaña, marking the 300th anniversary of the canonization of Saint Toribio de Mogrovejo. This Sunday, November 15, he travels to Cusco and Pucallpa, where he will meet with missionaries and representatives of Amazonian peoples; on Monday, November 16, he will celebrate the concluding Mass in Lima before departing for Rome.

items.title: [euronews.com] Denmark ratifies Greenland pact, clearing way for expanded U.S. military presence
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Denmark’s parliament on Nov. 19 ratified a security agreement with Greenland and the United States, clearing the final parliamentary hurdle for expanded U.S. military activity on the Arctic island. All 109 lawmakers present voted in favor after Greenland’s parliament approved the pact earlier in November. The Danish foreign ministry must now notify Washington by diplomatic note before the agreement takes effect; it does not require a U.S. Senate vote. The agreement, signed in New York on Sept. 22 by President Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen, supplements a 1951 defense accord. It allows the United States to expand operations at Pituffik Space Base and establish defense areas at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig, including for the proposed Golden Dome missile-defense system. The pact is to remain in force if Greenland becomes independent and reaffirms Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders’ right to self-determination. The deal followed months of tension after Trump repeatedly said the United States should control Greenland, at times refusing to rule out force. The agreement also restricts military installations to NATO members and aims to prevent China or Russia from gaining influence in strategic sectors. Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus said work would begin on legislation to screen outside investment on security grounds and on plans for the new U.S. facilities.

items.content_html:

Cyber incidents targeting operational technology (OT) systems—the controllers that monitor and operate physical equipment—have disrupted refrigeration, water and energy operations, often through exposed or outdated devices. Attacks on European supermarket refrigeration systems caused food spoilage, while incidents affecting U.S. water utilities and Polish energy organizations disrupted monitoring and control. French industry estimates put food waste and structural damage from the refrigeration attacks at tens of millions of euros. items.title: [Fast Company] A cyberattack forces you to pull the plug. Can your business keep running?
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

The recent cyberattack on European supermarkets sent the temperature in some Swedish freezers to a sweltering 131 F (55 C). The Dutch grocery chain Ahold Delhaize warned that a separate hack could strip up to 250 million euros ($277 million) from sales, and wipe as much as 100 million euros off operating profit in the fourth quarter. 

This recent spate of cyberattacks around the world, including a staggering $6.3 billion heist at the crypto exchange Binance, lays bare a blind spot in many boardrooms. Directors too often ask whether attackers can break into their systems. They should also be asking whether the business can take the hit and keep running.

Boards should assume attackers will get through. It’s a question of when, not if. And when they do, can the business still fulfill orders, pay staff, and keep critical facilities open? 

Too rare

Unfortunately, this is often not the case in the companies that I deal with. I recently worked with a board that had rightly grown more worried about cyber threats, and drafted in a former spy to carry out a cyber audit. The contractor ran penetration tests, hacked a few of the firm’s products, and found holes in its defenses. 

That’s fairly typical. The audit tested whether hackers could penetrate the company’s defenses. But it stopped short of testing whether the business could ride out a breach. And this is the gap I see running through many companies. 

Sometimes, stopping an attack from spreading means shutting down the very systems that keep you operating. 

Ahold Delhaize took some of its own websites and apps down as a precaution after the cyberattack, cutting off online shopping for some customers. The Dutch group contained most of the disruption within two weeks and it was getting back to normal once it reported third-quarter results. In Belgium, it had online shopping back up and running just a week after disclosing the breach. 

Contrast that with Marks & Spencer, the British retail stalwart. After a breach in April 2025, it stopped taking online clothing orders for a spell of 46 days. And when orders finally resumed, only part of its clothing range was available.

If you have to pull the plug on your own systems to contain a breach, how will you keep serving customers? 

The AI factor

AI is only raising the stakes. It’s my view that cyber threats have changed more in the past six months than in the previous six years. But many companies haven’t caught up.

Some of the newest crop of AI models are spotting security flaws that their predecessors missed, and have worked out how to exploit some of them. 

Take Anthropic’s Mythos Preview, which scored about 83% on a cybersecurity benchmark, compared with roughly 67% for the company’s previous best model, Claude Opus 4.6. Anthropic says it spotted thousands of security flaws, many of them serious, including in every major operating system and web browser. Worrying indeed. 

Last week, OpenAI released GPT‑6 Cyber to vetted customers. The model is designed to find security flaws and test whether they can be exploited.

The U.K.’s National Cyber Security Centre says the gap between a flaw becoming public and attackers exploiting it has already shrunk to just days. And it predicts that AI will compress that window further still, giving defenders even less time to patch the holes.

The most recent spate of supermarket hacks came on the heels of a similar hack of fridges at hundreds of French supermarkets. The result was piles of spoiled food, and fires even broke out.

Following that breach, Danfoss, the Danish industrial company that made the temperature controls, urged its customers to update their software and hardware. But just weeks later, hackers hit retailers using Danfoss controls again. This time, stores in several European countries were hit, including Sweden and Ireland.

Some fared better than others. Carrefour said it had installed updates and secured its connections after the first wave of attacks, steps it credited with curbing the numbers of its Belgian stores hit. Acting on the first warning helped Carrefour blunt the next attack.

Some retailers left their refrigeration systems exposed. That’s unacceptable. But even with tighter security, you still need a way to trade when the systems you depend on go dark.

What to do

Protect the operations you can least afford to lose. Then drill your teams on how to keep them running through an attack. When the malware designated NotPetya hit Maersk in 2017, the shipping giant handled about 80% of its usual volume manually. Staff taped paperwork to containers and took orders through personal Gmail accounts.

Consider a distribution center that needs to keep essential goods moving. Ask one team to fulfill a handful of priority orders without its usual order system or company email. Can staff confirm orders using a secure offline list and an agreed backup channel, check stock by hand and arrange transport? Have them log each dispatch on paper and check those logs against the order system once it’s back online.

When the drill ends, ask how much of the usual workload the team handled safely, for how long, and where it got stuck. Give each fix an owner and a deadline, then run the drill again.

Find out how long you can keep serving customers with your systems down. A real attack is a brutal way to get the answer.

items.title: [lemonde.fr] Costa’s EU budget draft cuts regional funds for first time
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

European Council President António Costa’s revised 2028-34 budget proposal would cut EU cohesion funding for the first time, reducing regional development funding by €8 billion compared with the Irish presidency’s previous draft. The change affects a coalition of 17 southern and eastern member states, including Poland, Italy and Spain, that had opposed cuts to cohesion funding. Costa’s proposal also reduces allocations for competitiveness, defence and external action. It leaves direct farm subsidies unchanged from the previous draft, but France says the proposed Common Agricultural Policy funding still fails to guarantee farmers’ income support. The revised framework cuts €204 billion from the European Commission’s original plan. EU leaders will discuss the proposal at a special summit in Brussels on November 26-27. The European Parliament must also approve the eventual budget, and its chief budget negotiator, Siegfried Muresan, has warned that lawmakers may withhold consent over the reductions.

European Central Bank policymakers held the deposit rate at 2.5% on Oct. 29, but President Christine Lagarde said they had seriously discussed a rate increase as energy prices and bond yields tightened financing conditions for households and businesses. Eurozone inflation reached 3.8% in September, and average 10-year government bond yields had risen about 35 basis points since the ECB’s September forecast. France’s 10-year borrowing cost topped 5% last week for the first time since 2002. The same day, Lagarde said she would leave the Frankfurt-based central bank on Feb. 7, 2027, before the end of her eight-year term, saying she wanted to speak on issues beyond monetary policy. Her departure opens a contest to lead the institution that sets interest rates across the euro area. Markets showed little reaction to the announcement, with analysts saying the ECB’s established practices were likely to outlast its president. Investors were pricing in three further rate increases by the end of 2027, which would bring the deposit rate to 3.25%. The ECB’s next policy meeting is scheduled for Dec. 17.

items.title: [elpais.com] Cyberattacks on refrigeration systems fuel concerns about connected household appliances
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Cyberattacks on internet-connected refrigeration systems in supermarkets and French blood banks have destroyed food in Europe and heightened concerns about connected devices. Nearly 800 freezers were sabotaged in France and Northern Europe this week. On November 2, temperatures also rose in the cold rooms of a blood donation service in France. There, alarms and swift action prevented damage to stored blood. The targeted systems used internet-accessible controls for maintenance and remote operation. According to experts, similar attacks on private smart-home devices are less likely because, with typical router configurations, the devices cannot be accessed directly from the internet. Risks include outdated software, weak passwords, and devices with cameras or microphones. Germany’s Federal Office for Information Security recommends automatic updates, separate networks for smart-home devices, and unique passwords. The identity of those behind the attacks remains unclear.

items.title: [theguardian.com] Arab lawmakers help elect Israeli parliament speaker, drawing Likud attack
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Israel’s Arab-led parties provided decisive support to elect Matan Kahana speaker of the Knesset, the Israeli parliament. Kahana, an ally of Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot, defeated Likud lawmaker Ofir Katz by 66 votes to 52, replacing Benjamin Netanyahu ally Amir Ohana after a debate lasting more than seven hours. Likud condemned the result as secured with “the votes of terror supporters,” while Eisenkot rejected a demand to bar Arab lawmakers from temporary deputy-speaker posts, saying there were no “type A and type B citizens” in Israel. The Arab-led parties together hold 19 seats; their support also features in negotiations over whether Eisenkot can assemble a governing majority. The opposition bloc has also taken control of key committees. Avigdor Lieberman, who chairs the temporary Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee, said he would summon security chiefs for oversight hearings, including on Iran. The rival blocs agreed to end a planned filibuster in exchange for postponing legislation to repeal the previous government’s judicial overhaul until Monday. Eisenkot’s mandate to form a government runs through Dec. 6, with a possible 14-day extension.

items.title: [prensa.com] Earthquake in Peru leaves one dead, 16 injured and 853 affected
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

The latest report on the magnitude 6.7 earthquake that struck central Peru on Friday put the toll at one dead, 16 injured, 853 people left homeless and another 529 affected. The deceased was a 45-year-old man who had been admitted to Hermilio Valdizán Medrano Regional Hospital in Huánuco; authorities did not specify the cause of his death. The report counted 152 uninhabitable homes and 156 damaged ones, as well as damage to six schools, 22 health facilities, four churches, three community centers and about 300 meters of roads. Huánuco, Pasco and Junín sustained the most damage; Lima and Callao were also affected. Authorities deployed medical personnel, ambulances, emergency response teams and technical crews, and coordinated humanitarian aid with local governments. In Huánuco, they sent machinery to clear roads blocked by rocks. Damage assessments and repairs to restore electricity are ongoing. The Geophysical Institute of Peru reported two subsequent earthquakes in Junín, with no new damage confirmed.

items.title: [cnbc.com] France-led protests spread to 31 European countries as rallies continue
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

France’s protest movement over living costs, wages and public services has spread to 30 other European countries, with more than 1,700 demonstrations recorded across the continent from Sept. 15 to Oct. 30, according to an analysis of Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED) figures. In France, the protests began with students challenging school conditions and widened to include unions and other groups. On Saturday, Nov. 7, the Interior Ministry counted 146,000 demonstrators nationwide, including 46,000 in Paris; unions estimated 250,000 and 75,000, respectively. It was the fourth consecutive Saturday of protests, and clashes followed in Paris and other cities. French authorities deployed about 70,000 security personnel on Saturday. The Interior Ministry recorded at least 360 arrests nationwide, according to AFP. Attendance was down from earlier weekends and from Thursday’s union rally, which drew 575,000 people by the government’s count. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu is due to meet labor unions and employer representatives on Monday, Nov. 9, to discuss wages and purchasing power. Student and teacher groups have called for a strike on Tuesday, while France’s Senate is scheduled to begin debating the government’s 2027 budget proposal on Nov. 20.

items.title: [brecorder.com] Projectiles hit two tankers near Hormuz as shipping traffic falls
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Unidentified projectiles struck two tankers sailing out of the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday, Nov. 21, near Oman’s Khasab, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO), a British maritime security agency, said. One tanker was hit on the stern about 11 nautical miles north of Khasab; the second was struck in its engine room about 17 nautical miles east. UKMTO reported no casualties and said the incidents might involve the same vessel. The environmental impact was unknown. Iran’s army said a tanker caught fire after hitting a naval mine in a restricted area east of the strait. It alleged that the vessel had switched off its identification and navigation systems. Reuters could not verify that account or establish whether it referred to either UKMTO incident. The U.S. military has said it cleared mines from the main shipping routes. The attacks occurred during the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, which began on Feb. 28. Iran has restricted passage through the waterway, while Washington has blockaded Iranian ports and escorted tankers. Before the war, nearly one-fifth of global crude oil supplies passed through the strait. Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said a Qatari delegation held two hours of talks in Tehran on Friday. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Iran’s demands must be met before discussing the strait’s reopening.

items.title: [lemonde.fr] France protests enter sixth weekend as turnout falls and clashes flare
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Protesters in France demonstrated over living costs and public services for a sixth consecutive Saturday on Nov. 21, with the Interior Ministry counting 82,500 participants nationwide and organizers estimating 150,000. Both figures were down from the previous weekend and far below the 800,000 organizers said had joined the first large march on Oct. 17. Students, unions, left-wing groups and Yellow Vest activists marched over living costs, housing, education and public services. Protesters also opposed a new law expanding legal protections for police who use firearms. Most marches were peaceful, but police used tear gas to disperse unauthorized gatherings in Lyon, and clashes and fires were reported in several cities. The Interior Ministry reported 144 arrests by 6 p.m. An AFP tally cited by French media counted at least 31 people seriously injured by security forces since the protests began; authorities have issued no official injury total. Youth- and worker-led rallies also took place in Portugal and Spain. French unions have called another public-sector strike and demonstrations for Dec. 1, demanding higher public-sector pay and renewed wage negotiations.

The six-to-five decision requires the Energy Ministry to reconsider the permits under proper procedures but does not order operators to stop work. Equinor’s Breidablikk and Aker BP’s Tyrving are producing, and Yggdrasil is scheduled to start production in 2027. Environmental groups Greenpeace Norway and Young Friends of the Earth brought the case against the state in 2023. The court said the oil companies were not parties to the case, so the ruling does not automatically suspend their operations. The campaigners’ lawyer said they would consider bringing a separate case against the operators. The ministry said it would re-examine the permits. The government has said it has changed its practice to include emissions from burning oil and gas in assessments for new fields.

items.title: [elpais.com] Leo XIV denounces racism against Afro-Peruvians and recalls slavery
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Pope Leo XIV denounced the discrimination that Afro-Peruvians continue to face on November 14 and recalled the slavery and humiliation suffered by their ancestors. He did so during a meeting in Zaña, a town in northern Peru recognized as a site commemorating slavery and African cultural heritage. Leo expressed his affection for the community and spoke about crime, extortion, and insecurity affecting families in the area. The pontiff, who was bishop of the Diocese of Chiclayo from 2015 to 2023, closed in Zaña the Jubilee Year marking the 300th anniversary of the canonization of Saint Toribio de Mogrovejo. In May, in his first encyclical, he had apologized on behalf of the Church for the role previous pontiffs played in legitimizing slavery in the Americas and for failing to condemn it for centuries. At the meeting, Analí Montenegro Mendoza, representative of the Afro-Peruvian community in the diocese, called for a Church in which no one feels inferior because of their skin color, history, or culture. Peru is the final stop on Leo's South American tour, which includes Argentina and Uruguay; he is expected to remain in the country until Monday, November 16.
